idiom_name: ThreadPoolExecutor(core, max, keepAlive, queue, factory, handler)
implementation_notes: Since Java 5 the JDK ships the pattern: Executors preconfigures the common shapes (newFixedThreadPool, newCachedThreadPool, newSingleThreadExecutor, scheduled variants) while ThreadPoolExecutor exposes the full policy surface - corePoolSize/maximumPoolSize, a BlockingQueue (ArrayBlockingQueue for a bound, LinkedBlockingQueue for an unbounded backlog, SynchronousQueue for direct hand-off), keep-alive for idle shrinkage, a ThreadFactory for thread names and daemon status, and a RejectedExecutionHandler (abort, caller-runs, discard) for overload. submit/execute plus the returned Future replace worker threads, the queue and the join; the queue choice is the real sizing decision, because an unbounded queue pins the pool at core size and turns overload into latency.
pitfalls: With an unbounded work queue the pool never grows past corePoolSize and maximumPoolSize has no effect: bound the queue if the bound is meant to be enforced.
Calling Future.get() from inside a pool task that waits on another task of the same pool deadlocks when the pool saturates (the javadoc's own example).
newCachedThreadPool is unbounded (SynchronousQueue, threads up to Integer.MAX_VALUE) and Executors' default threads are non-daemon: shutdown()/awaitTermination is mandatory or the JVM hangs.

variants.name: ForkJoinPool / CompletableFuture common pool
variants.idiom_name: ForkJoinPool with work stealing (or the common pool via CompletableFuture)
variants.implementation_notes: ForkJoinPool is a pool whose queues are per-worker deques with work stealing, designed for recursive divide-and-conquer tasks (RecursiveTask/RecursiveAction) and reused by parallel streams and by CompletableFuture's default async execution. Prefer it when the work decomposes recursively, because a worker that finishes its own deque steals from others instead of idling; recursive decomposition (fork/join) is what replaces the shared FIFO queue. Blocking inside a fork-join task needs ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker (or a plain executor), since stealing cannot help a task that is simply blocked, and the common pool is shared with the whole JVM.
pitfalls: The common pool is shared with parallel streams: saturating it slows unrelated library code.
A long-blocking fork-join task without ManagedBlocker can starve the pool; blocking I/O belongs in a plain executor.
join() swallows exceptions into the result flow while get() throws them - pick deliberately when wrapping.CompletionException appears.

variants.name: Virtual threads, one per task (Java 21+)
variants.implementation_notes: JEP 444 inverts the pooling advice for the blocking-I/O case: virtual threads are cheap enough that one is created per task (Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()), so the pool, its size and its queue disappear from the design and thread-per-request is again the simple, correct style - the runtime maps many virtual threads onto a small ForkJoinPool of carrier threads and unmounts them on I/O. Keep pooling platform threads when the goal is to bound concurrency against a limited resource; JEP 444 explicitly suggests a Semaphore for that instead of a virtual-thread pool, and warns that per-task state cached in ThreadLocals becomes per-task allocation.
pitfalls: Do not pool virtual threads (JEP 444): they are not scarce, and a pool re-introduces queueing without saving anything.
Pinning: a virtual thread inside a synchronized block or native call cannot unmount, so long I/O there occupies its carrier.
ThreadLocal caches silently become per-task copies and can multiply memory use with a million tasks.
